Firebase Security Rules Exposure Checker

Enter your Firebase project ID, plus its Realtime Database URL and/or one or more Firestore collection names. This sends real, read-only, unauthenticated requests and names which paths return real data with no login — the default-open / left-in-test-mode security rules exposure documented since Appthority's 2018 "Firebase mismanagement" report and still recurring today. Only run this against a project you own or are authorised to test.

Run the check

Firestore has no public "list every collection" endpoint the way the Realtime Database does, so name the collections your app itself reads — check your app's own source or its network tab. Leave this blank to check the Realtime Database only.

Enter a project ID and at least one of the two fields above, then click Check.

Report

Every path/collection checked

Path / collectionResultDetail

Prefer a CLI for CI, or does your browser block the Firestore check?

Same check, same modules, no browser — and never subject to browser CORS restrictions:

node check.mjs my-app-a1b2c --database-url https://my-app-a1b2c-default-rtdb.firebaseio.com --collection users --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if anything is exposed, so you can gate a deploy on it. Run it after every rules change and after adding a new collection: a rule that is correct everywhere else and missing on the newest collection is the ordinary way this reopens.

Common questions

Isn't my Firebase project's config supposed to be public?

Yes — the Firebase web config object (apiKey, projectId, databaseURL, and the rest) is meant to be embedded in your client-side app, and Google's own documentation says so explicitly. It identifies your project; it does not authorise access to it. Security Rules are the only thing standing between that public config and your actual data — a database left in test mode, or hand-written with a rule like allow read, write: if true, is readable by anyone who has ever loaded your app.

What actually goes wrong here?

Both Firebase products default new projects to a 30-day "test mode" with a rule that allows any read and write with no authentication, specifically so a team can build first and lock down rules before shipping. More background: why Firebase test mode exposes your data.

Is it safe to enter my project ID and database URL into this page?

Yes — both are already public. This page never sends either of them (or anything it reads back) to our servers: the Realtime Database request goes straight from your browser to your own project's REST endpoint, the same way your app's own client already talks to it. Still, only run this against a project you own or are authorised to test.

How is this different from the Firebase console's own Rules Playground?

The Rules Playground simulates a request against your rules source and needs you to be logged in as a project member. This tool sends a real, live, unauthenticated request to your project's actual REST endpoint from the outside — the same view an attacker, an external auditor, or a developer without console access would have.

Does a clean report mean my project is secure?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure — does an unauthenticated request return real data — at the Realtime Database root and at the Firestore collection names you name. It does not test authenticated roles, Cloud Storage buckets, Cloud Functions, write access, or any path/collection you did not list. Treat a clean report as evidence about what this run checked, not a full security audit.

How does this compare to just requesting the URL myself?

See how this compares to checking it by hand — the shallow, values-free read and the blocked-vs-unconfirmed distinction are easy to skip when eyeballing a raw request.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure at the Realtime Database root and the Firestore collection names you name. It never writes, updates, or deletes anything, does not test authenticated roles, Cloud Storage, or Cloud Functions, and cannot see an exposure at a path or collection you did not name. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the project has no exposure.

Nothing leaves your browser. The Realtime Database request goes straight from your browser to the URL you name — never through this site, and never logged or stored by us. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day — no project IDs, no database URLs, no collection names, no data contents, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Also worth a pass on your stack: Supabase RLS exposure checker covers the same "default-open unless a rule locks it down" shape for a different backend, Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker asks the same "does this storage hand out data with no login" question of AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage buckets rather than a Firebase project, and CORS misconfiguration checker and Security Headers checker cover other response-evidence classes in the same "read what's actually there, name the exact evidence" shape as this tool.

vs-requesting-the-url-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the Firebase Security Rules Exposure Checker

Firebase Rules Checker vs. requesting the URL by hand

Pasting a Realtime Database URL into a browser tab, or reaching for curl against the Firestore REST API, is a real and fast way to confirm the single obvious case: a root or collection that returns data with no login at all. Most developers who suspect a problem reach for this first, and it genuinely works for that case. This page is not affiliated with Google or Firebase — it names the Realtime Database and Firestore REST APIs only as the manual method anyone with the project ID could already try, not a product being compared against.

CheckBy handThis tool
Obvious open rootCatches itCatches it
Confirming exposure without pulling real dataA plain .json request returns real data — you'd read it to prove the pointUses shallow=true: key names only
Blocked path vs. genuinely empty oneBoth look empty unless you read the HTTP statusReported separately
Firestore's REST URL shape and document capEasy to get wrong or pull too muchOne document per collection, correctly formed
Several paths/collections at onceOne request at a timeAll named paths in one report
Repeatable in CIManual, point-in-timeReal exit code

When to still just check the URL

If you already suspect a specific path is wide open and just want to confirm it once, requesting the URL directly is fine — it's free and you already have the project ID. The gap this tool closes is doing that safely and completely: a shallow, values-free read of the Realtime Database, a capped read of every Firestore collection you name, a clear blocked-vs-unconfirmed distinction, and an exit code the same check can gate a deploy on next time.

Common questions

What does checking a Firebase project by hand actually show you?

Appending .json to a Realtime Database URL in a browser, or requesting the Firestore REST documents endpoint with curl, is a real, fast way to confirm the single obvious case -- a root or collection that returns data with no login at all. Anyone who knows the URL shape can do this in one request.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Three ways this scripted check catches and a by-hand request easily misses. (1) A plain .json request on an open Realtime Database pulls every field value under that path, not just key names -- proving the exposure this way means already doing the thing you were checking for; the shallow=true flag most people don't know to add avoids that. (2) A response of null or an empty object looks identical whether the path is genuinely empty or the rule is correctly blocking it, unless you also read the HTTP status code -- easy to skip when eyeballing a browser tab. (3) The Firestore REST endpoint's shape (documents/(default)/documents/<collection>) and its pagination field are not obvious from the console UI, so a first attempt at a manual request often gets the URL wrong before it gets an answer at all.

Why does this matter for CI, not just a one-time check?

A by-hand request is a point-in-time, manual look at one path or collection you remembered to try. Adding a new Firestore collection, or a rules change that is correct everywhere except the newest path, can reopen this exposure at any point after the last time someone thought to check. The CLI here returns a real exit code, so it can gate a deploy the same way a linter or test suite does -- catching the regression the day it ships rather than the next time someone happens to paste a URL into a browser.

why-does-firebase-test-mode-expose-my-da.text:
← Firebase security rules exposure checker

Why Firebase test mode exposes your data

Both Firebase products -- the Realtime Database and Firestore -- let you start a new project in test mode: a security rule that reads, in effect, "allow any read and write, no authentication required," so a team can build against real data before writing real rules. Firebase's own console warns that test mode expires after 30 days and reverts to fully closed -- but the warning is easy to miss, easy to dismiss, and easy to work around by simply extending the rule by hand once it expires, which converts a temporary convenience into a permanent, silent exposure.

What "open" actually means over the wire

Firebase's client config -- apiKey, projectId, databaseURL, and the rest -- is meant to be public; it identifies your project the same way a URL does, not a credential. The only thing standing between that public config and your actual data is the Security Rules attached to the Realtime Database and to Firestore. With a rule that allows read (and often write) to anyone, a plain unauthenticated GET to <databaseURL>/.json or to a Firestore collection's REST endpoint returns real data -- not a subset scoped to "your own" anything, to any visitor, including one who never logged in.

This is not hypothetical -- and it keeps recurring

Appthority's 2018 research, one of the first large-scale looks at this exposure class, found more than 2,300 mobile apps leaving a Firebase backend open this way, exposing tens of millions of records including passwords, health information, and financial data. That report is not a closed incident: the same underlying shape -- a database left in test mode, or a hand-written rule broader than intended -- keeps showing up in security research, bug-bounty write-ups, and breach disclosures in the years since, because the failure mode is structural rather than a one-time bug. Nothing in the SDK or the client stops a developer from shipping against an open database; only the rules do, and rules are opt-in.

Why this stays easy to reintroduce

A project can have correct, carefully written rules on 30 collections and a 31st, added in a later feature, that nobody wrote a rule for -- Firestore and the Realtime Database do not require every path to have an explicit rule before it can be read; an absent or overly broad rule simply falls through to whatever the closest matching rule allows. The Firebase console's own Rules Playground can catch this, but only for someone logged in as a project member who thinks to run it against the new path -- which is exactly the moment a live check from the outside, using only the project ID and database URL any visitor's browser already has, earns its keep.

Check your own project

A free tool that runs exactly the check above -- a shallow, read-only request to your Realtime Database root, and one capped request per Firestore collection you name -- is at the Firebase security rules exposure checker. It runs entirely in your browser for the Realtime Database half (or as a CLI for CI, and for Firestore if your browser blocks the cross-origin request), and never sends your project ID, database URL, or anything it reads back to any server of ours. As with any tool that sends requests to a project you name, only run it against one you own or are authorised to test.
